query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build platform and surrounding environment during the selective laser melting of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will reduce thermal gradients and facilitate stress relaxation, thereby minimizing residual thermal stresses and improving mechanical properties relative to standard ambient-temperature builds.
generation.material_initial_state: Atomized AlCrFeNiSi powder with a particle size distribution similar to 15–53 μm, as typically used for laser cladding or SLM of miniature components.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled preheating regime by elevating the build platform (and local build atmosphere) to an optimized temperature (e.g., between 600 °C and 800 °C) during processing.
generation.conditions: Selective laser melting (SLM) of miniature components using AlCrFeNiSi powder under an inert atmosphere; components are built on a preheated substrate compared to conventional builds at ambient temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in temperature gradients during melting and solidification, which lowers the rapid cooling rate and thereby minimizes the formation and retention of high residual thermal stresses.
generation.mechanism: Preheating slows down the cooling rate, allowing more uniform heat distribution and stress relaxation. This leads to fewer thermal contractions and reduced formation of microcracks or defects, ultimately improving mechanical properties such as ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the preheating intervention, components will exhibit lower residual stress levels, a finer and more uniform microstructure, improved ductility, and higher yield strength compared to components produced using conventional high-thermal-load, ambient-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Components fabricated via standard SLM processing at ambient substrate temperature, which typically results in high residual stresses and degraded mechanical properties due to rapid cooling.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to miniature components produced via SLM with AlCrFeNiSi powder where processing constraints like thermal management are critical; the intervention’s effects need verification within the specified process window (600–800 °C preheat) and for feedstocks with similar particle size distributions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheat temperature for balancing stress reduction with possible microstructural evolution in AlCrFeNiSi is not precisely known and may vary with slight compositional changes. Additionally, scaling to different component geometries might introduce further variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an experiment where two sets of miniature components are fabricated via SLM using identical AlCrFeNiSi powder and processing parameters, with the only variable being the build platform temperature. One set is processed under ambient conditions while the other is processed using a controlled preheat (e.g., 700 °C). Post-process the components and analyze residual stress (via X-ray diffraction), microstructure (grain size, defect density using optical and electron microscopy), and mechanical properties (tensile tests for yield strength and ductility).
measurements: Microstructure characterization (grain size, phase distribution, defect density via microscopy)
Mechanical properties (tensile testing for yield strength and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stress and a measurable improvement in mechanical properties and microstructural uniformity compared to the ambient temperature samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the last decades, additive manufacturing technologies have been increasingly used to produce metallic components with complex geometric shapes. One of the attractive additive manufacturing methods is selective laser melting (SLM), in which metal parts can be sintered directly based on a 3D model, regardless the of shape complexity, and sometimes without the need for tooling specific parts. Excellent characteristics can be achieved using SLM technology in various metallic materials, including aluminum alloys [,], martensitic steels [], and HEAs [,,,,,,,,,]. More recently, it has been shown that the SLM method has the potential to produce HEAs and MEAs with the TRIP/TWIP effect, which would have properties superior to counterparts obtained by other more conventional methods. Most of these studies were aimed at achieving a good combination of strength and ductility using TRIP and TWIP effects in SLM-derived alloys [,,,,,,].

H13 steel is an ideal choice for manufacturing molds and tools under high-strength and high-temperature working conditions due to its excellent thermal, mechanical, and processing properties. It can be undergo surface cladding for enhanced properties before use, or subjected to additive repair after prolonged use.
